finding: Test 16 requires that "Each §7 field takes its documented default, accepts both range endpoints, and rejects one step outside each", but two of §7's seven rows define no range and no numeric default: `runner` ("Built-in name or object", default `claude`) and `notify_cmd` ("Any command string", default unset). The test as written cannot be executed for 2/7 rows, and it also leaves the validation behaviour for those two undefined — is an unknown built-in template name a usage error, is an empty `notify_cmd` string equal to unset? Test 56 covers only the per-kind map and missing `cmd`.
suggestion: Restrict test 16 to the five numeric fields, and add a companion: "`runner` rejects an unknown built-in name as a usage error and accepts a runner object, a name, and a per-kind map; `notify_cmd` unset and set to an empty string are the same no-notification state."

finding: Test 53 asserts `tp audit --resolve`/`--resolve-all` dispose rows "on the same terms as their review counterparts" — but §3.3 defines a deliberate divergence: the audit selector "is a 0-based index or a `role:item_id` key, so a unit can name its own row without first locating its index", and §3.1.1 makes `role:item_id` the `audit-fix` unit's id, so the key form is the path every driver-spawned fix unit takes. A tester writing test 53 from its own text ships parity-with-review coverage and never exercises the key selector, its collision behaviour (two rows with the same `role:item_id`), or its miss behaviour.
suggestion: Split test 53: keep the parity claim for dispositions and `--force`, and add "an `audit-fix` unit disposes its row by `role:item_id` key without knowing its index; an unmatched key is an error, and the behaviour when two rows share a key is pinned."

finding: §10.7 states "no other command's exit codes change outside `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, which no current test sets", but §8a.4 changes `tp review --merge` and `tp audit --merge` from exit 0 to exit 1 for an input whose content lines all fail to parse — a documented current behaviour ("warn on stderr ... and still exit 0") that existing tests almost certainly pin. The invalidation inventory, whose whole job is to name the tests a change breaks, contradicts a required behaviour of the same release.
suggestion: Add the merge exit-code change to §10.7: name the assertions pinning `--merge` exit 0 on malformed input as moving in the same task as §8a.4, and narrow the blanket sentence to "no exit code changes beyond §8a.5's arity move and §8a.4's merge rule".

finding: "Every child is spawned with stdin closed" is a required behaviour (§2 lists it as the lesson taken from overnight practice: "backgrounded runs hang on stdin; ... §3.2 fixes stdin"), but no test in §10.1-10.6 asserts it. Test 37 enumerates the environment variables a child receives and tests 10/13 cover templates and dry-run; none inspects the child's stdin. The one failure mode the spec calls "the hardest unattended failure to diagnose" ships with zero pass/fail coverage.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: "A spawned child's stdin is closed: a seam runner that reads stdin sees EOF immediately rather than blocking, for both built-in templates and a configured runner object."

finding: "Caps are evaluated between iterations only. Children already spawned run to completion, so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration; the driver kills nothing" is normative and has no test. Test 3 asserts only that each cap produces its own `stop_reason`; test 41 asserts the no-kill behaviour for SIGINT/SIGTERM, a different trigger. Nothing pins that a cap tripping mid-iteration lets in-flight children finish, that their durable writes still land, or that the overshoot is bounded at one iteration — so an implementation that kills children on a cap, losing a task close, passes §10 as written.
suggestion: Add to §10.1: "A cap satisfied while children are in flight kills nothing: every in-flight child runs to completion and its durable write and run-state row land, no further unit is spawned, and the run overshoots by at most that one iteration."

finding: The oracle's `round` is never pinned to a meaning, and the whole round-directory addressing depends on it. §3.1.1 derives `TP_ROUND_DIR` = `.tp/rounds/<base>/$TP_PHASE-r$TP_ROUND` mechanically from it, but the kinds need different rounds: `review-role`/`audit-role` need the round about to be collected, while `review-resolve` and `audit-fix` operate on `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` of the round that was just recorded (§3.3). If `tp review --status`-style counting advances `round` the moment a round is recorded, every resolve/fix unit is handed a directory that has no `merged.ndjson` in it, its §3.3 predicate is trivially satisfied, and the loop advances rounds without ever disposing a finding. I cannot implement either the oracle or the driver without choosing one of these, and the two choices produce opposite loops.
suggestion: State explicitly what `round` reports at each point in a round-based phase (e.g. `round` is the round currently being worked — it advances only when the record unit has recorded and its findings are disposed), or give `next_units` entries their own `round` so a resolve/fix unit names the recorded round while role units name the next one. Add a test asserting a `review-resolve` unit's `TP_ROUND_DIR` contains the `merged.ndjson` the preceding `review-record` unit wrote.

finding: `next_units` entries carry `brief_command`, and §3.3 says "Each kind's brief comes from the `brief_command` the oracle supplies for it", but no section names a single one of the eight commands. The driver never executes them (§3.2.1) and the `{prompt}` text only says "run this unit's `brief_command`", so the oracle is the sole producer and I would have to invent every string: what a per-role review brief is (`tp review <spec>` emits all roles today, not one), what an `audit-fix` unit's brief is given its id is a `role:item_id` inside `merged.ndjson`, and what `review-resolve`, `decompose`, and the two record kinds get. These are not interchangeable choices — a per-role brief that emits the whole corpus defeats §3.3's per-role file contract, and a fix brief that does not carry the selector cannot reach `tp audit --resolve`.
suggestion: Add a per-kind table to §4.1 giving the exact `brief_command` the oracle emits for each of the eight kinds, including the flag that scopes a review/audit brief to one role and the selector form an `audit-fix` brief carries. If any of those flags does not exist yet, say so — it is a task in this release, not an assumption.

finding: §4.1's resume rule omits from `next_units` any role whose findings file satisfies §3.3's predicate, and §3.3 + test 59 make a zero-byte or blank-only file satisfy that predicate. The driver deletes a role's file immediately before spawning it (§3.1.1), so the file exists again only because the unit created it; a unit that creates it and dies before writing content (driver death, SIGKILL, harness crash) leaves a blank file that the next run reads as "role finished, found nothing". §8a.4 then exempts blank and zero-byte inputs from its exit-1 rule, so the record unit merges and freezes an undercounted round — exactly the dropped-role defect §8a.4 exists to eliminate, reintroduced through the resume path. The exit code that would distinguish the two cases lives only in the run state, which §3.5 forbids any decision from reading back, so no component can currently tell them apart.
suggestion: Separate "completed" from "present": have the driver write a per-role completion marker (e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-<id>.done`) after an attempt that exited 0 with its predicate satisfied, and make §4.1's skip rule test the marker while §3.3/§6.2's file-only predicate stays as-is for the Stop hook and the driver's in-run success test. State explicitly that a marker-less blank file is re-run.

finding: §5.1 pins the activation rule exactly — the mode is active when `TP_UNATTENDED` is "present, non-empty and not `0`" — and no test exercises any value but `1` and unset. Tests 19, 20 and 40 all use `TP_UNATTENDED=1` or its absence. The untested half is the fence-off half: whether `TP_UNATTENDED=0` and `TP_UNATTENDED=` leave the four user-only operations available. This is the boundary a mutation to the truthiness check would survive, and it is exactly the check that decides whether an unattended unit can raise its own round budget.
suggestion: Extend test 19 (or add a test in §10.3): "`TP_UNATTENDED=0` and `TP_UNATTENDED=` (empty) leave all four user-only operations exiting 0; any other non-empty value, not just `1`, refuses them with exit 2."

finding: Test 5 asserts "Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them, asserted from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps" — but nothing in §3.2.1's seam contract makes overlap observable. The seam's args are `{unit_kind} {unit_id} {log_path} {max_budget_usd}`; if the fake exits immediately, a correct concurrent driver can still produce non-overlapping timestamp intervals and the test fails spuriously, while a serial driver passes whenever timestamps tie. The assertion is timing-dependent rather than deterministic.
suggestion: Give the seam a deterministic rendezvous (e.g. the fake writes a start marker and waits for a barrier file, so N concurrent roles are only released once N markers exist) and restate test 5 as "all sibling role fakes reach the barrier before any exits; a non-role kind never observes another unit's marker".

finding: §10.7 says `tp resume`'s JSON shape gains `next_units` and `last_failure`, but §4.1 adds a third top-level key, `round` ("alongside `round`: the phase's current round number, or null"). Any test pinning resume's exact object set breaks on `round` too, and the sentence that decides which task carries those test moves does not mention it.
suggestion: List `round` alongside `next_units` and `last_failure` in §10.7, so the field and its invalidated assertions land in the same task.

finding: Round 18's single-writer rule (§3.5, line 283: a template using {log_path} 'owns the file, and the driver does not redirect') silently changes the TP_RUNNER_SEAM contract, but §3.2.1 was not updated with it. The seam's args are ["{unit_kind}","{unit_id}","{log_path}","{max_budget_usd}"] (line 152), so the seam is now a placeholder-using template and is no longer redirected; yet line 156-157 still says only 'The fake runner writes a final log line carrying that key' without saying where. Under the pre-repair text a fake that printed to stdout worked, because the driver redirected it; under the new rule such a fake produces no log file at all, so §3.2.2's read of the spend key from the final line (line 166) finds nothing and every spend/budget-cap test the seam exists to enable fails for a reason the spec does not explain.
suggestion: In §3.2.1, state that the seam's fake runner writes its final log line to the file named by its {log_path} argument (it owns that file under §3.5), not to stdout.

finding: The spend read has no error path. §3.2.2 covers only "a runner that declares no `spend_key`" (spend null, cap inert). It does not say what happens when a runner declares one and the log's final line is missing, not JSON, or lacks the key — the exact case a killed or crashed child produces. Treating it as 0 makes `cap-budget` silently under-count for the rest of the run; treating it as null contradicts "the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered"; treating it as a failed attempt would fail a unit whose durable write is present. All three are defensible and the run's budget arithmetic differs under each.
suggestion: State the rule: a declared `spend_key` that cannot be read yields `spend: null` for that unit, does not affect the unit's success test, and is surfaced in `--status` (e.g. a per-run count of unmetered units) so a partial total is never mistaken for a complete one — the same guarantee §3.2.2 already gives per-kind maps.

finding: Two run-start reporting claims are unverifiable as written: `run_max_budget_usd` being inert for a runner with no `spend_key` is "reported once at run start, not silently", and under a per-kind map "the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered". Neither the channel (stdout, stderr, run state, `--status`) nor the shape is pinned, and test 11 asserts only `spend` null plus an inert `cap-budget`. Two engineers write different assertions or none.
suggestion: Name the channel and shape (e.g. a `unmetered_kinds[]` key in the run-start line and in `--status`), and extend test 11: "a run whose runner declares no `spend_key`, and a per-kind map with one unmetered kind, each emit the documented unmetered notice naming those kinds exactly once at run start."

finding: The two merged.ndjson-based predicates are vacuously true on an absent file. `review-role`/`audit-role` predicates say "exists and every line parses"; `review-resolve` says "Every finding in `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` carries a disposition" and `audit-fix` says "That row carries a disposition in the round's results file" — neither states existence as a condition, so a unit that wrote nothing (or was handed the wrong round dir) satisfies its durable-write test by the empty-set reading and the driver records a success. §3.3's own rule that a predicate is "decidable by reading one file" does not say how a missing file decides.
suggestion: Say for each predicate what an absent file means. For `review-resolve` and `audit-fix`, require the file to exist and to hold at least one row, and make an absent `merged.ndjson` a failed attempt, not a pass.

finding: `review-resolve`'s durable write is "Every finding in `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` carries a disposition", and `audit-fix` disposes its row in that same file — while the round of record lives in `.tp-review/` (§3.3: "a review round file for `$TP_ROUND` exist"). The spec never says which of the two holds the authoritative disposition for a finding, so the same rows exist in two places with one of them accumulating state — the dual-source-of-truth drift §3.5 rules out for the run state, left unaddressed for findings, and a silent split of the existing `.tp-review/` state-dir contract.
suggestion: State in §3.3 (or §6.3) that `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` is the working copy resolution updates in place and `.tp-review/`'s round entry stores only counts/convergence derived at `--record` time — or, if `.tp-review/` also stores findings, say that re-recording after resolution refreshes them from `merged.ndjson`.

finding: Retry has no place in the loop. §3.1's six steps contain no retry step; §3.4 only gives the count (`1 + run_max_unit_retries`). Three things are therefore mine to invent: (a) whether a retry happens inside the iteration or via a re-poll of the oracle in the next one — test 17's "its role findings file is deleted before the attempt" implies driver-side, but §3.1.1 assigns that deletion to the oracle-returned set; (b) in a concurrent role batch, whether the driver waits for all siblings and then re-spawns only the failed ones, or re-spawns the whole batch; (c) where the attempt counter lives, since §3.5 forbids reading run state back, which means attempts are in-memory and reset on a driver death — making "exhausted its attempts" a per-process notion the spec never labels as such.
suggestion: Add a retry step to §3.1's loop that fixes all three: retries occur within the iteration, before the step-5 re-read; only the failed sibling is re-spawned; the attempt counter is per-run and in-memory, so a restarted driver starts a unit's attempts at 1 — and say that last part out loud, since it is a deliberate consequence of the no-read-back rule.

finding: §3.4 says "Caps are evaluated between iterations only. Children already spawned run to completion, so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" — but the same mechanism overshoots `run_max_units`, which the sentence omits. One iteration spawns a whole parallel role set (§3.3), and retries within an iteration each count as a spawned child (§3.4: "a retry counts again"), so a run can exceed `run_max_units` by up to (roles − 1) + retries. Reading the sentence literally leaves an implementer to check the units cap mid-iteration, which would either split a parallel role set or abort a retry — both contradicting §3.3 and §3.4's retry rule.
suggestion: Extend the overshoot sentence to name `cap-units`: "a run can overshoot its unit, wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration, because a parallel role set and a unit's retries are spawned without re-checking".

finding: Line 283 says the driver 'does not redirect' a template that uses {log_path}, but never says what becomes of that child's stdout and stderr. The pre-repair text had no such case: every child's streams went to $TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl. Inheriting them into the driver's own streams is the one outcome the paragraph's own rationale argues against ('Verbose command output ... is the fastest way to poison an agent's window'), and in an unattended overnight run it either floods the operator's terminal or is lost, which also leaves invariant 51's 'exit non-zero with the durable write absent' case undiagnosable.
suggestion: Add one clause to §3.5 fixing the disposition for the non-redirected case — e.g. the driver attaches that child's stdout and stderr to /dev/null, since the template has taken responsibility for the log — and mirror it in test 60.

finding: The driver's log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1.1 makes an `audit-fix` unit's id `role:item_id` — a colon, and whatever characters the auditor put in `item_id` (spaces, `/`). No sanitization or length rule is given, so one engineer tests the literal interpolation and another a slugified form, and on some filesystems the literal form is not creatable. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` has the same exposure if a role id ever carries a separator.
suggestion: State the derivation rule in §3.5 (e.g. every path component of an id is replaced by `-`, truncated at N characters, uniqueness preserved by `seq`), and add a test: "an `audit-fix` unit whose id contains `:` and `/` gets a creatable log path, and two ids differing only in those characters do not collide."

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1.1 defines an `audit-fix` unit's `id` as the finding's `role:item_id` — a caller-supplied composite that can carry `:`, `/`, spaces or path segments straight from an auditor's NDJSON row. The spec never says how an id is rendered into a filename, so a row whose `item_id` contains a separator writes outside `$TP_RUN_DIR` or collides with another unit's log, and the same id also reaches the run state's `units[].id`.
suggestion: State the sanitization rule once in §3.5: the log filename uses `<seq>-<kind>` plus a sanitized id (non-`[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced), while `units[].id` keeps the unsanitized value; add a test asserting an `audit-fix` id containing `:` and `/` produces a log path inside `$TP_RUN_DIR`.

finding: `run_state` distinguishes `in_flight` from `crashed` by whether `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` is held, while the same paragraph's neighbour says "Neither sub-mode takes the run lock." With flock there is no read-only "is it held" call: the only portable probe is a non-blocking acquire, which does take the lock when free (and must then release it), and which on some platforms succeeds for a lock the *same* process already holds. As written the two sentences cannot both be implemented literally.
suggestion: Say the probe is a non-blocking acquire that is released immediately, and that "takes the run lock" in the neighbouring sentence means "holds it for the duration" — or replace the lock probe with a liveness check on a pid recorded in the run state, and drop the no-read-back exception it would need.

finding: §4.1 says `next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` "render `next_units[0]` when the array is non-empty", and test 38 asserts only that rendering. What those three fields hold when `next_units` is `[]` — the two `no-units` cases of §4.1 (blocked work, awaiting an operator decision) and the `release` phase — is unspecified, and those are precisely the states an operator reads after an unattended run stops. Only `next_action.summary` is pinned for them.
suggestion: State the empty-array rendering in §4.1 (e.g. `command`/`brief_command`/`payload` are null while `summary` names what the phase awaits), and extend test 38: "on a blocked phase, an operator-decision phase and `release`, `next_action` carries the documented empty-array shape."

finding: §4.2 now names both writers of `last_failure` but leaves the clearer anonymous: "a success clears it only when `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matches". Neither writer can be it by symmetry — `tp done` cannot know the unit succeeded (its durable write is checked afterwards, §3.3), and the driver is the only component that evaluates success, but §4.2 never says so. It also does not say whether a *successful* `tp done` inside a still-unfinished unit clears a record the driver wrote for that same `(unit_kind, unit_id)` on a previous attempt, which is the common case for a retried `implement` unit.
suggestion: State that the driver is the sole clearer, on a unit that passed both halves of §3.3's success test, and that no other command clears the file — so a `tp done` mid-unit never erases the record its own retry is supposed to read.

finding: "one that fails schema validation, is judged by its §3.3 predicate" makes escalation detection turn on a validation whose rules are unstated: which of `{decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at}` are required (is `options` optional, is `phase` required outside a round-based phase?), whether `decision` must be one of the five listed values, whether unknown keys invalidate, and whether `unit_kind`/`unit_id` must match the unit whose seq names the file. That last one matters most: without it, a unit can escalate on another unit's behalf and stop the run.
suggestion: Name the validation exactly: required keys, `decision` restricted to the five values, unknown keys ignored, and `unit_kind`/`unit_id`/`phase` must equal the driver's own values for that seq or the record is invalid. Add it as an explicit assertion in test 22.

finding: Every unit pays for two overlapping orientations in the same fresh context. The SessionStart hook injects `tp resume --compact` unconditionally ("deliberately does not branch on the matcher"), and §3.2.1's fixed `{prompt}` then orders the unit to run its own `brief_command` as its first act. Both payloads name the phase, the unit's subject, and — per §4.2 — `last_failure`, which the spec says is surfaced by `tp resume` AND `tp brief`. The spec never says what `tp resume --compact` strips inside a run, so on the plugin path the whole handoff is emitted twice per unit, and the double emission scales with every unit of a 100-unit run rather than once per session.
suggestion: State the division: either the SessionStart hook skips its injection when `TP_UNIT_KIND` is set (the brief is the unit's authoritative orientation and arrives anyway), or fix `tp resume --compact` to emit only what the brief does not — and in either case say once, in §4.2, which of the two carries `last_failure` so it is parsed once per unit.

finding: "Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped" is a precise output contract with no test in §10. Test 14 covers `tp run --status` shapes but never the compact form, and §10.7 does not list it either. The claim is also the only place `--compact` is mentioned for `tp run`, so which sub-mode accepts the flag (`--status` only, or the driver too) is left open.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: "`tp run --status --compact` keeps `run_id`, `phase`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals and omits the `units` array and every `log_path`; the driver mode rejects/accepts `--compact` as documented."

finding: `location_clusters` entries are `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` but the meaning of two fields is not pinned: `count` could be the number of findings at that location or the number of distinct roles, and `severities[]` could be the per-finding severity list (ordered, with repeats) or the deduped set. Test 28 asserts only that a location reported by two roles under different classes is grouped, so both readings pass. Ordering of `roles[]` and of the cluster array itself is also unspecified, which makes a golden-fixture assertion non-deterministic.
suggestion: Pin it in §8a.1: `count` is the number of findings in the cluster, `severities[]` is the deduped set in fixed severity order, `roles[]` is sorted, and clusters are ordered by `location`. Then extend test 28 to assert a three-finding two-role cluster reads `count` 3 with a two-element `severities[]`.

finding: `location_clusters` is a derived index with no named consumer in this release. §4.1 fixes the driver's machine surface at `next_units`, `round` and `phase` — "the driver parses those three and nothing else" — and §8a.1 itself states the entries change no arithmetic, no `clean` flag and no `--status --check` exit code. Meanwhile the bytes are not free: `--merge` is what a `review-record` unit runs and its stdout lands in that agent's window, and `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` restates fields the same merged record set already carries verbatim. The motivating measurement (63 co-located blocking findings) describes a human misreading, and a human is by definition not in the loop during the unattended run this spec builds.
suggestion: Name the consumer and the moment it reads the key, or shrink it to what nothing else carries: omit the key entirely when no location clusters, drop `severities[]` and `count` (both re-derivable from the records in the same payload), and emit clusters on `--status` only, where an operator is actually reading.

finding: The `{unit_id}` and `{unit_kind}` placeholders duplicate `TP_UNIT_ID` and `TP_UNIT_KIND`, which §3.1.1 guarantees unconditionally in every child's environment. Neither built-in template uses them — `claude` is `["-p", "{prompt}", …]` and `opencode` is `["run", "{prompt}"]` — so their only exercised use is the `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` fake, i.e. a surface that exists to be tested. They nonetheless carry documentation, a resolver, the exit-2 unresolved-placeholder path and part of test 10. `{prompt}`, `{max_budget_usd}` and `{log_path}` each carry something no env var does (a composed instruction, a flag the runner must see in argv, ownership of the log file); these two do not.
suggestion: Drop `{unit_id}` and `{unit_kind}` and let the seam read the env like any other runner, or name the concrete runner shape that must take them positionally — a wrapper that cannot read its own environment — so the knob is justified rather than assumed.

finding: §5.1 fences `runner` "at any layer" because it names a command the driver executes, yet §3.2.1 defines `TP_RUNNER_SEAM`, an environment variable that supplies the runner's `cmd` and "outranks every layer of §7's precedence, including a CLI flag", and §5.1's env-layer rule only covers `TP_` + field name (`TP_RUNNER`). The seam is therefore an unfenced route to the value §5.1 fences most strictly; the only thing closing it is the unstated fact that a child cannot mutate the already-running driver's environment.
suggestion: Say in §3.2.1 that the seam is read once from the driver's own environment at start and is therefore unreachable from any unit, and add the same sentence to §5.1's fence paragraph so the exception is visible where the fence is stated.

finding: Two of the run-state fields store what the file already determines. `log_path` is fixed by §3.5 as `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` for both template forms — the redirecting form and the `{log_path}`-owning form receive "that same path" — so it is a function of `seq`, `kind` and `id`, three fields already in the same row; and `run_state: stopped` restates `stop_reason != null`, which the same `--status` payload prints, leaving the lock check to distinguish only `in_flight` from `crashed`. The row array is rewritten atomically twice per attempt, so a run at `run_max_units` 10000 rewrites a redundant string 20000 times for a file the spec says no decision ever reads back.
suggestion: Derive `log_path` at read time from `seq`/`kind`/`id`, keeping a stored value only if a future template is allowed a path the driver did not compose (in which case say so); and either document `run_state` as purely a convenience alias for the `stop_reason`/lock pair or reduce it to the distinction the lock actually resolves.

finding: `phase` in the `last_failure` object is a function of `unit_kind`: each of §3.3's eight kinds belongs to exactly one phase (`implement`; `review-role`/`review-record`/`review-resolve`; `decompose`; `audit-role`/`audit-record`/`audit-fix`). The object is surfaced by both `tp resume` and `tp brief`, so the redundant key is emitted and parsed on both paths, and it also forces `tp done` — the second writer — to depend on `TP_PHASE` for a value it could compute from the `TP_UNIT_KIND` it is already keyed on. §3.1.1 correspondingly ships `TP_PHASE` to every child with no consumer named anywhere in the spec except this derivation and `TP_ROUND_DIR`, which the driver composes itself.
suggestion: Drop `phase` from the record (or state explicitly that it is a denormalized convenience and which reader needs it in that form), and either name a consumer for `TP_PHASE` or drop it from §3.1.1's variable list.

finding: §5.1 fences four decision families (skip-gate, round-cap raises, `import --force`, and — added in this spec — raises of `run_max_*` plus any setting of `runner`/`notify_cmd`), but §5.2's `decision` enum covers only the first three, leaving the run-cap and runner/notify cases to `other`. The driver stops the same way either route, but the operator-facing record loses the one field that names which fenced decision was hit, for exactly the decisions this version introduces.
suggestion: Add `raise-run-cap` (covering `run_max_*`) to §5.2's enum, or state explicitly that the run-cap and runner fences escalate as `other` because they are operator-configuration rather than cycle decisions.
